name: Tenochtitlan
info: Tenochtitlan was the Mexica capital on an island in Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, founded in 1325 by the date now accepted, capital of the Aztec Empire, and captured by the Tlaxcaltec and the Spanish in 1521.

facts.founded: By the Mexica on a small island in Lake Texcoco; the exact date is unclear, and 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 for the 600th anniversary
facts.where: On an island in what was Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico, now the historic centre of Mexico City, Mexico
facts.known: Capital of the Aztec Empire; the Templo Mayor; the chinampas; causeways and canals; the market of Tlatelolco; the palace of Moctezuma; the fall of 1521
facts.today: Its ruins lie in the historic centre of Mexico City, which Cortés founded on the site.

t: The Mexica built Tenochtitlan on a small swampy island in Lake Texcoco, enlarging it with chinampas, and it became the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas.
As capital of the Aztec Empire in the 15th century it had causeways, canals, aqueducts, a walled ceremonial centre of about 45 buildings and a population estimated at 200,000 to 400,000.
Cortés besieged it for over 90 days, disease struck its people, and it fell on 13 August 1521 to the Spanish and Tlaxcaltec; Mexico City was founded on the ruins.
dyk: In 1987 archaeologists found 1,789 human bones five metres below a Mexico City street, a burial of the 1480s at the foot of the main temple of Tenochtitlan.
ev: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, by the date now given
The levee of Nezahualcoyotl is completed under Moctezuma I
Tenochtitlan fights a war against its neighbour Tlatelolco
Ahuitzotl begins to rule, and the city is rebuilt after a flood
Hernán Cortés arrives in the city on 8 November
The city falls on 13 August to the Spanish and Tlaxcaltec
Major excavations of the Templo Mayor begin

sections.origins:
Tenochtitlan, also called Mexico-Tenochtitlan, was a Mexican altepetl built on an island in what was then Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico. It was one of two Mexica altepetl, or city-states, on the island; the other was Tlatelolco. The name is traditionally thought to come from the Nahuatl tetl, rock, and nōchtli, prickly pear, and is often read as "Among the prickly pears growing among rocks". One late 16th-century manuscript, the Bancroft dialogues, suggests the second vowel was short, so the etymology remains uncertain, and it is also thought that the city was named after Tenoch.

The exact date of the founding is unclear. The date 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 to celebrate the 600th anniversary of the city, and the city is dated from 1325. According to the Mexica state religion, the wandering tribes awaited the fulfilment of an ancient prophecy: they would find the destined site for a great city, signalled by an eagle with a snake in its beak perched on a cactus (Opuntia), which had grown from the heart of Copil. The Mexica saw this vision on what was then a small swampy island in the lake. The image is now on Mexico's coat of arms and flag.

Undeterred by the unfavourable terrain, they set about building their city. They used the chinampa system, misnamed floating gardens, for agriculture and to dry and expand the island, which was perpetually enlarged as the city grew. The city lay on the western side of the shallow Lake Texcoco, the largest of five interconnected lakes.
sections.growth:
The Mexica came to dominate other peoples around them, and Tenochtitlan grew into the largest and most powerful city in Mesoamerica. Commercial routes brought goods from as far as the Gulf of Mexico, the Pacific Ocean and perhaps even the Inca Empire.

The city's water was managed with large works. During the reign of Moctezuma I a levee, called the levee of Nezahualcoyotl and reputedly designed by him, was built. It was estimated at 12 to 16 kilometres long and was completed about 1453. It kept fresh spring-fed water around the city and the brackish water of the lake beyond it to the east. Two double aqueducts of terracotta, each more than 4 kilometres long, brought fresh water from the springs at Chapultepec. After a flood of the lake the city was rebuilt during the rule of Ahuitzotl, between 1486 and 1502, in a style that made it one of the grandest in Mesoamerica.

The city covered an estimated 8 to 13.5 square kilometres. There are no precise figures for its population, which has been estimated at between 200,000 and 400,000, and some popular sources go as high as 350,000. One of the few comprehensive academic surveys of Mesoamerican city sizes reached 212,500 people living on 13.5 square kilometres. Only Paris, Venice and Constantinople might have rivalled it among European cities, and it was said to be five times the size of the London of Henry VIII. It is also said that Moctezuma ruled an empire of almost five million people in central and southern Mexico, gaining tribute and prisoners to sacrifice to the gods.
sections.rulers:
Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Mexica, founded in 1325, and in the 15th century the capital of the Aztec Empire. Its rulers included Moctezuma I, under whom the levee was built; Axayacatl, in whose reign the calendar stone was carved around 1470 and who was the predecessor of Tizoc; Ahuitzotl, who ruled between 1486 and 1502; and Moctezuma II. The highest social class, the teteuctin, were the rulers of various parts of the empire, including the king.

The city fought its neighbour Tlatelolco in 1473, a war told in the Anales de Mexico y Tlatelolco. The two city-states are later named together as Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco.

The Spanish took the city in 1521. Hernán Cortés founded the Spanish capital of Mexico City on its ruins, and for a time this ciudad de españoles was called Mexico-Tenochtitlan. The Spaniards set up a cabildo, or town council, with jurisdiction over Spanish residents. The outer Indian section, renamed San Juan Tenochtitlan, continued to be governed by the previous indigenous elite and was divided into the same subdivisions as before, and Santiago Tlatelolco likewise had its own municipal council throughout the colonial period. Each kept jurisdiction over settlements on the mainland that supplied labour and tribute demanded by the Spanish, though those settlements gradually gained their own rulers. The city later became a cabecera of the Viceroyalty of New Spain.
sections.life:
The city was divided into four zones, each divided into 20 districts, the calpulli, which were crossed by streets and divided by canals with wooden bridges that were removed at night. Three main streets led to causeways to the mainland at Tepeyac, Iztapalapa and Tlacopan; Bernal Díaz del Castillo reported them wide enough for ten horses. Bridges in the causeways let canoes pass and could be pulled away to protect the city.

In the centre, inside a walled square 500 metres to a side, stood about 45 public buildings, among them the Templo Mayor, dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc, the temple of Quetzalcoatl, the ball court with its tzompantli, or rack of skulls, and the Sun Temple. Outside it stood the palace of Moctezuma with 100 rooms, each with its own bath, and nearby the cuicalli, or house of the songs, and the calmecac. The palace held two houses for animals, with about 300 people to care for them, a botanical garden and an aquarium.

Each calpulli had its own market, and the main market at Tlatelolco, according to Cortés, was twice the size of Salamanca with about 60,000 people trading daily; Bernardino de Sahagún gave a more conservative 20,000 on ordinary days and 40,000 on feast days. Society was highly stratified: macehualtin commoners, pipiltin nobles, cuauhipiltin eagle nobles, the highest teteuctin, tlacohtin slaves or indentured servants, and the hereditary pochteca merchants, who paid no taxes but sponsored the feast of Xocotl Huetzi. Status showed in houses of reed and mud, adobe brick, or stone masonry.
sections.crises:
Hernán Cortés arrived in Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519. Moctezuma II chose to welcome him as an ambassador rather than risk a war that aggrieved indigenous people might join. Cortés later detained Moctezuma, after an episode in which two Spanish officers sent to Qualpopoca at Nueva Almería were captured and killed, and Moctezuma was supposedly the one who had ordered it. During the festival of Toxcatl, Pedro de Alvarado, left in charge, feared a surprise attack, tortured three men until they said it was planned, and had the Spaniards come heavily armed and close every exit of the courtyard.

Cortés besieged Tenochtitlan for over 90 days, causing a famine. On 13 August 1521, after over two months of fighting, the city fell to the Spanish and their Tlaxcaltec allies, which ended the Aztec empire. Cortés then directed the systematic destruction and levelling of the city, despite opposition, and began its rebuilding.

The people of the city were also exposed to diseases to which they had no immunity. Symptoms were often delayed for up to ten days, then the infection spread through the body, causing sores, pain and high fever. People were too weak to move or obtain food and water, burying the dead became difficult or impossible, and the death toll rose steadily over the next 60 days. Many native residents died during the siege, though the indigenous population kept a strong presence in the city.
sections.legacy:
Cortés founded Mexico City on the ruins, and the site kept symbolic power as the capital of the Aztec empire, which Cortés sought to appropriate. The Templo Mayor was dismantled and the central district of the Spanish city built over it, and the great temple was destroyed by the Spanish during construction of a cathedral. In the Spanish traza, a European-only zone of 13 blocks in each direction of the central plaza, streets were laid out in a chessboard pattern, while the indigenous districts were irregular and built of modest materials. A royal hospital for indigenous residents was founded.

The location of the Templo Mayor was rediscovered in the early 20th century, but major excavations only took place from 1978 to 1982, after utility workers came across a stone disc 3.25 metres across showing the dismembered body of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui. The ruins were built over seven periods, and their weight has made them sink into the lake sediment, so they now rest at an angle. In August 1987 archaeologists found 1,789 human bones five metres below street level, a burial dating to the 1480s at the foot of the main temple.

Mexico City's Zócalo stands at the site of the original central plaza and market, and many of the old causeways still correspond to modern streets. The calendar stone, 4 metres across and over 18 tonnes, carved about 1470, was found in the ruins. The ruins lie in the historic centre of Mexico City, and the World Heritage Site of Xochimilco holds what remains of the geography of the Mexica capital: water, boats and floating gardens.

summary: Tenochtitlan was the Mexica capital on an island in Lake Texcoco, the centre of the Aztec Empire in the 15th century. After a siege of over 90 days and an epidemic it fell to the Spanish and Tlaxcaltec in 1521, and Mexico City was founded on its ruins.
references: Michael D. Coe, Mexico: From the Olmecs to the Aztecs (Thames & Hudson, 2008)
Bernal Díaz del Castillo, The Conquest of New Spain (Penguin Books, 1963)
Jacques Soustelle, La vida cotidiana de los aztecas en visperas de la conquista (Fondo de Cultura Economica, 1984)
notes: The article is short: the rulers section rests on a few names and on the colonial arrangements, and says nothing of how Tenochtitlan's relation to Tlatelolco changed after the 1473 war.
The article never names smallpox; it speaks of 'diseases to which they had no immunity'. I did not name the disease. It gives no death figures for the siege or the epidemic.
Internal tension: the siege lasted 'over 90 days' (conquest section) but the fall on 13 August 1521 came 'after over two months of fighting' (colonial section). Both given as the article gives them.

The article's Toxcatl passage says only that the Spaniards came heavily armed and closed the exits; it does not state what followed, and I did not add it. It also does not say what became of Moctezuma II.

The lead says the city fell to 'the Tlaxcaltec and the Spanish'; the article says nothing more of the allies. The founding year 1325 is marked circa because the article says the exact date is unclear.

Wanted but not found: casualty figures for the siege; the fate of Moctezuma II; the end date of the Aztec Empire beyond 1521; the number of rulers; the article's own 'Mexica' versus 'Aztec' usage is mixed, kept as given.
